meaning: The 'stop' radical walks along the 'going' path, but at the 'ten' point it stops and adds a 'dot' — that dot is the tiny trick or technique that turns a plain walk into a special skill.
reading: ジュツ — Imagine a 'jutsu' master (like a ninja) who uses his art to stop a tree with a single dot — the tree freezes, and he says 'JUTSU!'

meaning: An upside-down box sits on top of a mouth, and below that a stop and a going — the stop and going are the walking parts, and the box-mouth is a narrow opening between buildings. This is the alley you walk through.
reading: The alley is so narrow you have to 'toe' your way through — imagine your big toe scraping both walls as you walk. (トウ = 'toe')

meaning: A vertical stroke and two splayed strokes sit above a stop and a going — the splayed strokes are like two walls leaning together, and the stop and going show you walking between them. This is the lane.
reading: In this lane, a 'ko' (cow) blocks the way — you have to stop and wait for it to move. (コウ = 'ko' as in cow)

meaning: The 'going' radical walks along the 'soil' path, but the 'stop' radical blocks it — so you have to stop and look around: this is a busy boulevard or street in a town, where going is interrupted by crossings and shops.
reading: ガイ — Imagine a 'guy' (ガイ) standing on the street corner, waving at you to come over to his town's main boulevard.

meaning: A government office is where the 'going' (行) of official business happens, but you must first pass a 'stop' (彳) at the gate, which is marked by a 'one' (一) and a 'five' (五) on a 'vertical stroke' (｜) — like a numbered checkpoint. The 'mouth' (口) at the top is the clerk's window where you state your business.
reading: The government office is where you go to get your 'ga' (ガ) — like a loud 'gah!' of frustration when you see the long line. Imagine shouting 'GAH!' at the clerk's mouth.

meaning: A going (行) path with a stop (彳) on one side and a mouth (口) and month (月) on the other — this is a narrow lane or alley, where you stop to talk and time seems to slow.
reading: You walk down the alley and hear a 'ko' (コ) sound — a cat meowing from a doorway.

meaning: A mouth (口) shouting a warning, with tanned leather (韋) armor, and going (行) with a stop (彳) — this is the defense that guards the city walls.
reading: エイ — Imagine a knight shouting 'hey!' (ei) as he raises his leather shield to defend against an attack.

meaning: A going (行) path with a stop (彳) on one side, and on the other side you see two short strokes on top (并), an eye (目), and oneself (自) — the path you see with your own eyes, leading to your neck (首). This is the way or path you choose.
reading: You follow the path and say 'to' (トウ) — 'to the way!' — as you march forward.

meaning: A vertical stroke hits the going shape, and a day and a ri are in the middle — the stroke collides with the road, causing a brunt at the highway. The stop and strike parts show the impact.
reading: ショウ — Picture a 'show' (ショウ) where two cars collide head-on — the crash is the brunt of the impact, and the highway is blocked.

meaning: A towel and a mouth are guarded by going and stop — the going and stop parts patrol around the towel and mouth, defending them.
reading: The defense force shouts 'エイ!' like a battle cry — 'EI!' as they hold the line.

meaning: Going (行) with a stop (彳) and a large (大) rice field (田) inside a wrapping enclosure (勹) — you measure the field's balance with a scale, finding equilibrium.
reading: The scale goes "KO!" (コウ) as it tips — like a karate chop "KO" to the balance.

meaning: Going and stopping meet at an old bird's eye — the crossroads where all paths converge, watched by the bird.
reading: At the crossroads, you say 'coo' (ク) to the old bird, and it points the way.

meaning: A lid (亠) sits on top of a garment — like a hat on a coat, the lid is the collar of the clothes.
reading: You put on your clothes and say 'EE' (イ) — the sound of a satisfied sigh as you dress.

meaning: Look at 初 (beginning) — the left side is a piece of clothing with a collar and two hanging sleeves, like a shirt draped over a hanger, showing it's the clothes radical.
reading: ころも — Say 'koromo' — imagine a kimono that 'corrals' your body, wrapping you in a warm 'koromo' robe as you put it on.

meaning: A garment (衣) hangs over a gentleman (士) standing on soil (土) under a lid (亠) with two (二) marks — this is the surface you see, like a chart or table laid out flat.
reading: The surface of the table is covered in a bright 'hyo' (ヒョウ) — imagine a giant 'hyo' printed on a chart, like a loud poster.

meaning: For the first time, you use a dot and a right hand to open the seam of your garment.
reading: You sigh (sai) in relief as the seam opens.

meaning: A thin kimono is like a first-time garment with three stripes.
reading: The thin kimono is so thin you can see the sun (san) through it.

meaning: A garment (衣) hangs from a lid (亠) with a single line (一) through it — the fabric is thinning and tearing, so the garment's strength declines and it begins to wane.
reading: The suit (スイ) you wear is old and fraying — its power slowly declines, like a fading suit.

meaning: The first time a person sews, they use an upside-down box to hold the thread — that's how you mend a priest's vestment.
reading: ノウ — The priest's vestment is 'now' (like 'now') being mended, and the person says 'now' it's fixed.

meaning: The first time you wear something, it's the day you put on your everyday underwear — it's your daily layer.
reading: ジツ — The everyday clothing is a 'jits' (like 'jits' in 'jitsu') — it's your real, daily 'jitsu' (truth) of comfort.

meaning: Inmost heart is a garment (衣) with ten (十) mouths (口) – ten secrets hidden inside.
reading: チュウ sounds like 'chew' – you chew on your inmost thoughts.

meaning: The family name (氏) is standing at the first time (初) in front of a dish (皿) that only has a tiny drop (丶) of blood (血) — so there's merely a hint of it, not a full offering.
reading: The family name (氏) is 'key' (キ) to unlocking this rare character — think of a key turning in a lock, and the sound 'ki' clicks in.

meaning: The first time (初) the king (王) and a gentleman (士) met, the king's robe had a gusset (衽) at the neck, and the gentleman noticed the extra cloth folded in.
reading: The gusset (衽) is like a 'jin' (ジン) — imagine a genie (ジン) popping out of the neck of a robe, stretching the gusset wide.

meaning: A garment with a lid on top, and a hat on a one — that's your quilt, pulled up to your chin.
reading: キン — The quilt is so warm it makes you 'kin' (キン) with comfort, like a cozy king.

meaning: A hat on top (个) of a first time (初) — the collar (衿) of a coat is like a hat for the neck, and the one (一) line of the collar wraps around.
reading: The collar (衿) is where you hang a 'kin' (キン) — picture a golden 'kin' (キン) coin clipped to the lapel, shining at the neck.

meaning: A long garment (衣) hangs down, but a mouth (口) is buried in the soil (土) below — the kimono is so long it drags through the dirt.
reading: The long kimono is worn by 'en' (エン) — like 'en' as in 'en-gawa' (縁側), the long veranda where you wear it.

meaning: The first time (初) a person (人) with a large (大) build and two (二) arms (ユ) — the sleeve (袂) hangs down from the shoulder like a wide cloth, and the foot of a hill is its edge.
reading: The sleeve (袂) swings like a 'tamoto' (たもと) — imagine a 'tamago' (たまご) egg rolling out of the sleeve, but it's a 'tamoto' (たもと) that holds it.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a lid (亠) and a mouth (口) and power (力) — the lid is the collar, the mouth is the pocket, and the power is the coarse fabric that feels strong.
reading: The coarse camlet robe is worn by a monk who says 'KE' (ケ) — like 'kay' — as he bows.

meaning: A garment (衣) is draped over a person at the side (化) who is piling (弋) things under a lid (亠) — that's a sack or bag you carry.
reading: タイ — Think of a 'tie' (タイ) closing the top of the bag, tying it shut with a rope.

meaning: The first time you see this coat, it has a wrapping enclosure around the body, but the stop inside says it's not for moving — it's a padded coat, not armor.
reading: ホウ — The coat is so huge it makes you say 'whoa' (ホウ) as you put it on.

meaning: The first time you bare your shoulder, you expose the day (日) and the one (一) — a single line of skin from neck to waist, stripped to the waist.
reading: タン — You strip to the waist and 'tan' (タン) your chest like a drum in the sun.

meaning: A first time on a rice field — the sleeve of your shirt brushes the crops as you walk, giving them the cold shoulder.
reading: シュウ — 'Shoe!' (シュウ) — the sleeve caught on my shoe as I walked.

meaning: The first time you see this thin kimono, it has a hat on top (个) and three (彡) threads of embroidery running down — so thin you can see the hat's shadow through it.
reading: シン — The thin kimono is so sheer you can 'shin' (シン) through it like a ghost.

meaning: The first time you tie a warrior's headband, the white (白) cloth wraps around your forehead — the white stands out against your face, marking you as a fighter.
reading: バツ — The headband is so tight it gives you a 'batsu' (バツ) mark — an X — on your forehead.

meaning: The first time you strap on greaves, you see a dot (丶) on the knee, a sweeping stroke (ノ) down the shin, a right hand (又) pulling the strap, and a piling (弋) of padding — all under the first time cloth.
reading: ハツ — The greaves make you 'hats' (ハツ) — like a hatch — opening your legs to run.

meaning: The first time you pull on socks, you see a tree (木) — the sock is like a tree trunk for your foot, with one (一) big toe sticking out at the top.
reading: バツ — The socks are so mismatched they give you a 'batsu' (バツ) — an X — on each foot.

meaning: A lid sits on top, with a mouth and two splayed strokes inside, all wrapped in a garment — this is the emperor's ceremonial robe, so ornate it has a mouth and strokes as decorations.
reading: コン — Imagine the emperor in his imperial robes saying 'コン' (con) as in 'conqueror' — he conquers all lands while wearing these robes.

meaning: A book cover is like a satchel: the large part (大) wraps around the first time (初) pages, held by a one (一) and a sweeping stroke (ノ) strap — a bag for a book.
reading: The book cover is a 'cheat' (チツ) — you sneak a cheat sheet inside it. Imagine a student hiding a cheat sheet in the book cover.

meaning: A garment with a lid on top, a one, a sweeping stroke, and a large shape inside — this is a book cover or satchel, a large cloth bag that holds things under a lid.
reading: チツ — Picture a satchel that is 'チツ' (chitsu) — like 'chit' — a small note you stuff into the bag, and the bag is the cover for your book of chits.

meaning: A summer kimono is short clothing: the first time (初) you wear it, you see the two (二) short strokes on top (并) and the ten (十) stitches holding the vertical stroke (｜) — it barely covers you.
reading: In summer, you wear a 'han' (ハン) — like 'han' in 'hanami' (flower viewing) — you're outside in a light short kimono, sweating in the heat.

meaning: A garment with a halberd and a lid on top — the halberd's shaft measures the length of the garment, so this means 'length'.
reading: ボウ — Imagine measuring the length of a garment with a 'ボウ' (bow) — a long bow, and you stretch it along the cloth to see how long it is.

meaning: The sleeves and cuff are the part of the robe that touches the soil (土) when you bow — the first time (初) you kneel, the katakana-mu shape (厶) of the cuff drags in the dirt.
reading: The cuff is 'kyo' (キョ) — imagine a 'kyo' (like 'key-oh') — you use a key to unlock a cuff that's too tight, twisting it off.

meaning: A first time (初) you wear a pelt (皮) as a cover, and a right hand (又) pulls it over you — you incur the weight of it, like a veil or brood over something.
reading: ヒ — A 'he' (ヒ) sheepishly pulls a pelt over his head to hide, incurring a sneeze.

meaning: An ancestral shrine has embroidery: the first time (初) you visit, you see the little (小) offerings and the 乞-shaped part (乞) begging for blessings, with a sweeping stroke (ノ) hanging over the shrine.
reading: The ghost kanji is 'ne' (ネ) — like 'neigh' — a ghost horse neighs at the ancestral shrine, its embroidered cloth flapping in the wind.

meaning: A garment with a mother and a 'do not' on top — the mother says 'do not' go out without a hood, so this is a hood or cover for the head.
reading: ほろ — The mother puts a 'ほろ' (horo) — like 'hollow' — hood over your head, making a hollow space that covers you like an awning.

meaning: A person at the side and a dog, both wrapped in a garment — this is a cloth wrapper, used to wrap up a dog or a person's belongings for the first time.
reading: フク — The wrapper is 'フク' (fuku) — like 'fuku' as in 'fukubukuro' (lucky bag) — you wrap a lucky bag in this cloth, and it brings fortune.

meaning: A first time (初) wearer puts on a large (大) two (二) layered skirt, wrapped with a wrapping enclosure (勹) at the waist — that's the men's formal divided skirt.
reading: The skirt swishes 'KO' (コ) as the man walks — 'KO, KO' — like a drumbeat under the formal robe.

meaning: A garment with a king and a person at the side — the king's garment has a neck piece, and the person at the side adjusts the gusset or gore at the neck.
reading: ジン — The king's neck is 'ジン' (jin) — like 'gin' — he wears a gin-soaked collar, and the gusset holds it in place.

meaning: A mouth (口) speaks to a first time (初) wearer, who puts a hat on top (个) of the kimono and ties it with one (一) sash — that's a lined kimono, with an extra layer inside.
reading: The lined kimono is made for the cold, so you say 'コウ' (kou) — like 'cold' but with a 'k' — as you shiver in it.

meaning: A gentleman (士) at his first time (初) at a ceremony uses a mouth (口) to call for help, then holds up his long sleeves with his hands — that's 'hold up'.
reading: You hold up your sleeves to keep them clean, saying 'ケツ' (ketsu) — like 'ketchup' — but you're holding up the hem, not the sauce.

meaning: A woman (女) with a mouth (口) complains about her first time (初) wearing this — it's torn and patched, so it's just 'clothes' (old rags).
reading: The torn clothes make you say 'ジョ' (jo) — like 'Joe' — as in 'Poor Joe, his clothes are all ripped.'

meaning: Soil (土) is on the hem of this ancient ordinary kimono, because it's worn for everyday work — not for fancy occasions, just a simple robe.
reading: This ancient kimono is 'ケイ' (kei) — like 'kay' — as in 'Okay, it's just an old everyday robe, not special.'

meaning: A box (囗) holds a large (大) mat, and this is your first time (初) seeing it — it's a mat, coverlet, or underwear, all rolled up in that box.
reading: You unroll the mat and say 'イン' (in) — like 'inn' — as in 'I'm staying at an inn, and this is my mat.'

meaning: A lid (亠) sits over soil (土), with the katakana-mu shape (厶) beside it, all under a halberd (戈) that cuts through a garment (衣). The halberd slices the fabric to tailor a pattern, and the judge's decision is that cut.
reading: The judge's gavel falls with a crisp "SAI!" (サイ) as he cuts the case short, like scissors snipping cloth.

meaning: A 'garment' (衣) gets caught on a 'reap' (刈) hook, and a 'bare bone' (歹) pokes through a 'lid' (亠) — the cloth splits and tears.
reading: レツ — Imagine tearing a cloth with a loud 'RETS' (レツ) sound, like ripping paper.

meaning: A divining rod (卜) is held by a samurai in old ceremonial garb, and it's his first time (初) wearing it — the rod is part of the formal outfit.
reading: The samurai's garb is called 'かみしも' (kamishimo) — say 'kami' like 'god' and 'shimo' like 'snow' — so picture a god in snow wearing this formal robe.

meaning: The 'going' part (行) is on the left, and the 'first time' (初) is on the right. Imagine you're measuring a sleeve for a kimono — the sleeve length is how far the 'going' (行) of the fabric extends, and it's the 'first time' (初) you've measured it, so you note the length.
reading: The reading is ゆき (yuki). Picture a snowy 'yuki' (snow) day, and you're measuring the sleeve length of a coat — the snow falls on the sleeve, and you say 'yuki' as you measure.

meaning: A gentleman (士) puts on a garment (衣) under a lid (亠) and a left-side kata (爿) — that's his disguise, his attire for pretending to be someone else.
reading: Imagine a SO (ソウ) — a tiny sewing kit — stitching a fancy dress (attire) for a costume party, where everyone pretends.

meaning: A 'garment' (衣) with a 'bird' (鳥) perched on it, and under the 'lid' (亠) there are 'four dots at the bottom' (杰) — the bird's tail feathers curl upward as it sways. The whole image is a bird on a coat, gently wavering in the breeze.
reading: The bird's tail curls up like a 'cho' (チョウ) — think of a 'chow' dog's tail curling up as it wags. The garment sways, and the dog's tail is the same curling motion.

meaning: Two short strokes on top of a mouth, then beans, and the first time — the beans are the rough cloth, and the first time a boy servant wears this cotton outfit, he spills beans on it.
reading: The boy servant's cotton clothes are so short they show his 'shu' (shoe) laces — imagine his ankles sticking out. (シュ = 'shoe')

meaning: A person and a large thing are inside the first time — the large person is wrapped in a lined garment, with the lining showing at the collar. The person is large because the garment is padded.
reading: The lined garment is so warm you wear it in the 'ko' (cold) — imagine shivering until you put it on. (コウ = 'cold' but with a 'ko' sound)

meaning: A box with a tree inside, and the first time — the tree is the dress, and the box is the border or band that wraps around its edge like a fence. The band is the box that holds the tree (the dress) in place.
reading: The border band is 'kon' — like a 'cone' of thread used to sew it on, rolling around the edge of the dress.

meaning: A sweeping stroke, a mouth, soil, and a king, all on the first time — the king stands on soil, and the sweeping stroke is his robe falling off. He takes off his clothes and exposes his body to the soil.
reading: The king takes off his clothes and stands naked — you say 'tei' (like 'tay' in 'stay') as he stays there exposed in the open.

meaning: A garment (衣) has a lid (亠) on top, but underneath it is the ri (里) — the back side, the reverse of what you see.
reading: The 'ri' in 'river' flows behind the garment — you can't see it from the front, it's in the back. (リ)

meaning: Under a 'lid' (亠) you see a 'mortar' (臼) — you use it to grind and collect grains. The 'garment' (衣) at the bottom is the cloth you spread out to gather the ground flour. So you collect and assemble everything into the cloth.
reading: You gather all the flour into a pile and say 'hou' (ホウ) — like 'hoe' — you use a hoe to scrape the grains together into the mortar. The hoe is the tool for collecting.

meaning: A 'garment' (衣) has a 'lid' (亠) on top, and below it a 'mouth' (口) with 'a pair of legs' (儿) sticking out — that's the descendant, the hem (border) of the family line. The 'upside-down box' (冂) is the border frame around the whole thing.
reading: The descendant stands at the border of the family, and you say 'ei' (エイ) — like 'aye' — a sailor's 'aye' as he looks out to the border of the sea. The descendant is the 'aye' who continues the line.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a hat on top (个) and a mouth (口) that speaks of first time (初) abundance — the valley (谷) is rich, with two splayed strokes (ハ) of plenty flowing down.
reading: ユウ — Picture a rich valley where you shout "YOU!" (yu-u) to a friend across the abundant fields — the sound 'yu-u' is in 'you' (pronounced 'yuu').

meaning: A 'garment' (衣) with 'water' (水) and a 'dot' (丶) on top — the dot is a drop of rain, and the water soaks the leather. Under the 'lid' (亠) you have the water, making the leather clothing heavy and wet.
reading: The leather coat is so heavy with water you say 'kyuu' (キュウ) — like 'cue' — you need a cue to prop yourself up because the coat is too heavy. Imagine a pool cue holding you upright.

meaning: A sweeping stroke of cloth hangs from the first time you wear it, like a flag flapping at your hem — the mouth of the skirt opens wide, revealing underwear beneath.
reading: The skirt's hem sweeps like a 'coon' (クン) tail dragging on the ground, catching dirt as you walk.

meaning: A 'garment' (衣) is wrapped and bound by a 'hook stroke' (乙) that loops around it, and under the 'lid' (亠) there's a 'mouth' (口) with a 'stop' (已) — the binding stops at the mouth. The 'comma-design' (巴) and 'home country' (邦) are the pattern on the cloth, but the hook is what wraps it all up.
reading: You wrap the book in a cloth bag and tie it with a hook — you say 'ou' (オウ) like 'owe' — you owe someone the book, so you wrap it up to return it. The hook binds it tight.

meaning: A person at the side (化) uses a cliff (厂) and grass on top (艾) to supplement a ten (十) and a utilize (用) with a dot (丶) — filling in what's missing.
reading: You supply extra parts to a robot, and it goes "HO-ho!" like a happy helper — ホ.

meaning: A gentleman (士) puts on a garment (衣) under a lid (亠) and a left-side kata (爿) — he's dressing up, but also pretending to be someone else.
reading: ソウ — Imagine a 'sow' (pig) wearing a fancy garment and pretending to be a princess — she's dressed up and pretending.

meaning: A Buddhist surplice is a garment (衣) with a little (小) water at the side (汁) and a lid (亠) on top — like a robe that drips with holy water.
reading: サ — Think of 'sah' (like 'saw') — you saw a monk's surplice flapping in the wind as he walks.

meaning: The first time you see inside a ri (village), you find the reverse — the palm and sole are hidden within, not outside.
reading: You flip the inside out to find a 'ree' (リ) — a small reef hidden in the palm of your hand.

meaning: A gentleman (士) in his first time (初) wearing a garment (衣) needs help adjusting it, so you lend a hand to help him.
reading: The gentleman's helper is a 'hee' (ヒ) — like a horse neighing 'hee' as it helps pull the garment straight.

meaning: A coverlet is a garment (衣) you pull over your head — it has a vertical stroke (｜) and two (二) lines, an upside-down box (冂) with a mouth (口) and soil (土) — like a blanket with a dirt pattern.
reading: チュウ — 'Chew' — you chew on the edge of your coverlet while you sleep, like a nervous habit.

meaning: A right hand (又) holds a needle to mend the first time (初) tear in a garment (衣) — you patch it up.
reading: You 'tack' (タツ) the cloth with quick stitches — like tacking a sail, 'tatsu' sounds like 'tack-sue' but the 'tack' is the mending action.

meaning: To mount maps or scrolls — you take a garment (衣) and paste it with a lid (亠) and soil (土) — like using cloth and mud to stick a scroll to a wall.
reading: ヒョウ — 'Hyo' (like 'hi-yo') — you say 'hi-yo' as you hoist a heavy scroll to mount it on the wall.

meaning: An upside-down box (冂) sits on top of a first time (初) robe, with a vertical stroke (｜) and one (一) line marking the ancient robe's long, layered shape.
reading: The ancient robe is worn by a 'ryo' (リョウ) — imagine a samurai named Ryo putting on this robe for the first time.

meaning: A garment with a crown and a lid, and an esteem inside — the skirt is so highly esteemed it gets a royal crown on top, and the mouth below is the hem that speaks elegance.
reading: ショウ — Imagine a skirt that shows a 'SHOW' — a fashion show where the model twirls, and the skirt flares out like a crown.

meaning: A garment with a lid on top, and un- on the side — the long robes are so long they are 'un-' practical, trailing behind like a river, with the lid keeping the head covered.
reading: ハイ — Picture long robes that make you say 'HI!' (ハイ) as you trip over them — you wave your arms and shout 'HI!' while falling.

meaning: A lid on top, then a garment, then un- — the flowing gown has a lid for a hat, and the un- part is the wind that blows it sideways, making it flow.
reading: ハイ — Imagine a flowing gown that looks like a 'HI' sign — you see the gown and say 'HI!' to the person wearing it, but they just flow past.

meaning: First time (初) in a rice field (田) under a tree (木) — you're naked, with no clothes, just the field and tree as your cover.
reading: You're 'HADAKA' (はだか) — imagine saying 'HA-DA-KA' as you shiver, naked in the cold field.

meaning: A garment wraps around a rice field, with a lid on top and two splayed strokes as ties — you wrap the field in cloth, cover it with a lid, and tie it with the two strokes to hide it.
reading: ホウ — Picture wrapping a rice field in a garment and shouting 'HO!' (ホウ) as you toss it over your shoulder like a sack — 'HO!' the heavy bundle.

meaning: A sweeping stroke and a day sit under a not, all wrapped in a wrapping enclosure — to bare the shoulder, you must first unwrap that enclosure and let the day's heat hit your skin.
reading: You bare your shoulder to show off a tattoo of a 'セキ' (seki) — like a 'sexy' shoulder, but with a hard K sound.

meaning: A garment (衣) is cut by a reap (刈) tool, with a cow (牛) and a towel (巾) under a lid (亠) — this is the process of manufacture.
reading: セイ — Say 'say' (セイ) as you watch a factory 'say' out products, each one made in a specific place.

meaning: A flag (尸) hangs over a mouth (口) and ten (十) — but the first time (初) you see it, you notice the hem of a robe dragging on the ground, like a mountain's foot.
reading: The hem swishes as you walk — 'so-so' (ソ) — like the sound of fabric brushing the floor, and the mountain's foot is 'suso' (すそ).

meaning: A first time, soil, and a divining rod combine — this ancient ordinary kimono is so plain that even the soil and rod used to divine its pattern look boring.
reading: You wear this kimono to a 'ケイ' (kei) — like a 'cage' — but it's so ordinary that you feel trapped in it.

meaning: A vertical stroke, three stacked strokes, a one, a first time, and a woman — the skirt's hem is like a woman's first attempt at stacking layers, with a single vertical line holding it all together.
reading: The skirt's hem is 'つま' (tsuma) — like 'tsunami' but shorter — imagine a tiny wave of fabric curling at your feet.

meaning: The first time (初) you see a stooping figure (夂) and the 乞-shaped part (乞) next to a day (日), you realize it's a duplicate of something you've seen before.
reading: フク — Imagine a 'fuku' (a lucky charm) that comes in duplicate — two identical charms side by side.

meaning: A vertical stroke (｜) and one (一) mark a door (戸) that is the first time (初) you see a narrow passage, with a tome (冊) and a flag (尸) squeezed together by two hands (廾) — the space is narrow and small.
reading: The narrow path makes you say 'HEN' — like 'hen' (a chicken) that can barely squeeze through a crack.

meaning: A car (車) drives over a crown (冖) that sits on the first time (初) you wear a loincloth — the cloth is tied around your waist like a car's seatbelt.
reading: The loincloth is tied tight, and you grunt 'KON!' — like 'con' (a convict) who wears a simple cloth in prison.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a grain stalk (禾) hanging from a lid (亠) and a tree (木) — imagine a robe with sleeves so long they sweep like grain stalks, flowing from the shoulders.
reading: シュウ — 'shoe' — you slip your arms into the ample sleeves like putting on a pair of shoes, and the sleeves flow down to your feet.

meaning: A garment with a long, flowing sleeve — the top part shows a rice field under a lid, and below is the garment itself, suggesting sleeves that hang down like a field of cloth.
reading: The sound is そで (sode) — imagine a sleeve (sode) swinging as you wave, like a 'so-dee' cheerleader's pompom made of cloth.

meaning: The first time (初) you see a day (日) wrapped in a wrapping enclosure (勹) with a spoon (匕) beside it, you realize it's a brown woollen kimono — the color of dried earth.
reading: The woollen kimono is so rough it makes you say 'KATSU' (like 'cats') — imagine petting a cat made of brown wool, it's scratchy.

meaning: A garment (衣) covers a person at the side (化) who has a mouth (口) and a little (小) lid (亠) — the person is wearing a fancy robe, and the mouth praises them for it.
reading: You praise the person by saying 'HO' as you bow, and they blush under their robe.

meaning: A garment (衣) for a baby's first time (初) — the diaper is wrapped around like a tree (木) trunk, with a person at the side (化) holding the baby's mouth (口) clean.
reading: You change the diaper with a 'ho' (ホ) of surprise at the smell.

meaning: A shirt with a decorative collar — the left side is a garment, and the right side shows a person at the side (化) with a hat (个) and a reaped (刈) month (月) pattern, like a fancy shirt with a collar that stands out.
reading: The sound is ユ (yu) — picture a shirt that says 'you' on it, like a custom shirt with the word 'you' printed in big letters.

meaning: A ceremonial gown (衣) for a queen, made of tanned leather (韋) — the first time (初) she wears it, she opens her mouth (口) to give a royal decree.
reading: The queen's gown is so grand it makes everyone say 'ee' (イ) in awe.

meaning: A first time (初) you see a cloth pasted together — the month (月) and a spoon (匕) are stuck on a vertical stroke (｜) over one (一) line, like layers of paper glued flat.
reading: ハイ — “Hi, I’m pasting paper!” — imagine a paper-pasting craftsman waving “Hi” as he layers cloth.

meaning: An old man (老) stuffs a bag with soil (土) and a day (日) worth of supplies, using a sweeping stroke (ノ) to tie it shut — that’s your valise.
reading: チョ — “Cho” like “chow” — you stuff the bag with chow (food) for the trip.

meaning: A thin kimono — ten (十) threads of esteem (尚) woven into a rice field (田) pattern, worn as an undergarment for the first time (初).
reading: タン — “Tan” like “tan” skin — you wear this thin undergarment to get a tan.

meaning: A robe (衣) that is a first time (初) use of a dish (皿) on a day (日) — picture a ceremonial robe worn only on the first day you use a special dish.
reading: ウン — 'oon' as in 'moon' — the robe is so thick and padded it feels like you're wearing a full moon, round and warm.

meaning: A cushion (褥) made of a garment (衣) with a measurement (寸) and a dragon (辰) — imagine a dragon-sized mattress measured out in cloth, with the sign of the dragon embroidered on it.
reading: ジョク — 'joke' — the cushion is so soft that sitting on it is a joke, you sink right in and can't stop laughing.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a spoon (匕), a katakana-mu shape (厶), and a month (月) — picture a robe with a spoon and a crescent moon sewn on, worn by someone too dull to know they look silly.
reading: ダイ — 'die' — the stupid person wears the robe so foolishly that you'd rather die than be seen with them.

meaning: A lid over fire and an ear, all wrapped in a garment — this is a light overcoat, so thin you can see the fire and ear through it.
reading: The light overcoat is so thin it makes you say 'ケイ' — like 'KAY' as in 'OK, it's just a light coat.'

meaning: A garment (衣) that is crowded (込) with northeast (艮) — imagine a robe stuffed in a crowded drawer, its color fading from being pressed against the northeast corner.
reading: タイ — 'tie' — the color fades like an old tie that's been washed too many times, losing its brightness.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a divining rod (卜), a pair of legs (儿), a spoon (匕), a cliff (厂), and tiger spots (虍) — picture a robber on a cliff, using a divining rod to spot a tiger-spotted robe, then running down on legs to snatch it with a spoon.
reading: チ — 'cheese' — the robber says 'cheese' as he grabs the robe, grinning for the camera before running off.

meaning: A lid over water and a buy, all inside a garment — you buy water and carry it in your bosom, wrapped and concealed in your sleeve.
reading: You carry the water close to your chest and say 'カイ' — like 'KAI' as in 'I'll keep it safe in my kai (pocket).'

meaning: The dotted cliff (广) is the top of the pants, the first time (初) you put them on you pull them up over your car (車) — so this is trousers.
reading: The 'コ' sound is like 'ko' in 'cowboy' — picture a cowboy pulling up his コ (ko) pants over his horse.

meaning: A dot, a sweeping stroke, a lid, an upside-down box, an open box enclosure, the katakana-mu shape, the name of a chinese emperor, and first time — all tangled in a garment, this is a bridal veil, a first-time covering for the bride.
reading: The bridal veil flutters and you say 'リ' — like 'LEE' as in 'the bride's veil is a lovely lee (shelter) for her face.'

meaning: Feathers and white and ice, all folded with first time — the pleats in the garment are like folded feathers, white as ice, made for the first time.
reading: The pleats are folded like a 'ショウ' — imagine a show (ショウ) where the pleats fan out like a peacock's feathers.

meaning: A woman's first time wearing a torn garment leaves only rags — the mouth of the sleeve is frayed, and the vertical stroke of the one thread hangs loose.
reading: The rags are so old they smell like a 'roo' (kangaroo) — you'd toss them in the bin. (ロウ)

meaning: A garment (衣) is covered with soil (土) and dry (干) dirt, and two short strokes on top (并) show it's been stepped on — it's dirty and ragged, so you undress it.
reading: チョウ — Imagine a dirty garment that you throw into a chopping bowl (チョウ) to wash, but it comes out even more ragged.

meaning: A garment (衣) is stained with soil (土) and a dot (丶) of filth, under a lid (亠) — it's so filthy you treat it with irreverence and throw it away.
reading: セツ — Picture a filthy garment that you set (セツ) on fire to burn, because it's too dirty to keep.

meaning: A pleat is a fold you make by eye — you see the two splayed strokes of the crease, then the shellfish shell pattern repeats like a tuck in cloth.
reading: The pleat is so sharp it could 'seki' (sake) you — a fold that cuts like a knife. (セキ)

meaning: A diaper is a cloth wrapped around a baby's bow — the insect and the katakana-mu shape are the messy parts you must clean, first time every time.
reading: The diaper is so full it makes you 'kyo' (cough) — you hold your breath. (キョウ)

meaning: A garment is wrapped around a mouth that is open wide, while a tree grows from the lid on top — the whole scene is so wonderful you must praise it aloud.
reading: ホウ — Imagine a loud 'HO!' of praise echoing from the mouth, bouncing off the tree and lid, as if the garment itself is cheering 'HO-uh!'

meaning: A vertical stroke (｜) rises from a well (井) under a lid (亠), wrapped in a garment (衣) with two splayed strokes (ハ) — this is the act of rising, lifting up.
reading: The garment rises up as you 'jo' (ジョウ) — like 'jo' (as in 'jog') — you jog up the hill, raising your arms.

meaning: A first-time garment has a large hood made from two short strokes on top, with a vertical stroke and a dot, and a sweeping stroke crossing a bow — all bundled into a cowl.
reading: ホク — Picture a hooded figure saying 'HOK-ay, I'm ready!' as they pull the cowl over their head, the bow and pike hanging from the hood.

meaning: A first-time garment is so thin you can see the rice field through it, with a mouth and ten grains of rice scattered on the field — it's just an undergarment.
reading: タン — Think of a thin kimono that goes 'TAN!' when you snap it — the sound of the fabric stretching over the rice field.

meaning: A first-time garment is mixed with an old bird and a tree — the bird perches on the tree, and the garment is tangled in the branches, everything blended together.
reading: ザツ — The old bird squawks 'ZATZ!' as it gets tangled in the mixed garment and tree branches, a messy blend of feathers and cloth.

meaning: A first-time garment is a raincoat, with two splayed strokes on top, a dot and a sweeping stroke, and a table with a right hand holding a pike — all protecting against the rain.
reading: ハツ — The raincoat goes 'HATZ!' as the pike hits the table, and the right hand pulls the hood tight against the storm.

meaning: A first-time garment is stretched over a large frame, with rice and an upside-down box — the opaque sliding door hides the rice inside the box, covered by the garment.
reading: オウ — Slide the door with a long 'OH-uu' sound as it glides over the rice, the upside-down box muffling the noise.

meaning: Two splayed strokes (ハ) and two short strokes on top (并) sit above a crowded (込) first time (初) — and a pig (豕) is wrapped in these grave clothes, laid out for burial.
reading: The grave clothes are so fine they make you say 'sui' (スイ) — like 'sweet' but with a sigh, as you lay the pig to rest in its final outfit.

meaning: The garment is thick and fine, like a dragon's robe. The first time you see it, the sign of the dragon is embroidered on the衣, and the lid and cliff above it show it's a ceremonial piece.
reading: ジョウ — Imagine a 'joe' (a regular guy) who suddenly wears fine clothes, but he trips on the long hem and falls off a cliff.

meaning: The garment's front flap flutters in the wind. The first time you see it, the say-part is on the flap, and the wrapping enclosure holds it, but the pair of legs below are shaking from the vibration.
reading: セン — A 'sen' (a coin) is tied to the hem of the apron, and as it flutters, it clinks against the two splayed strokes, making a shaking sound.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a lid (亠) on top, a flag (尸) sticking out, and a mouth (口) with ten (十) spicy (辛) things inside — all folded into pleats and creases, like a wrinkled cloth with many layers.
reading: ヘキ — The pleats are so sharp they make a 'hekki' sound when you run your finger along them, like a quick 'heck' of surprise at the crisp fold.

meaning: Show (示) two (二) little (小) first-time (初) trees (木) — the collar of a shirt is like a little forest of fabric around the neck.
reading: The collar is tight, so you say 'KIN' (キン) — imagine a king (キン) wearing a stiff golden collar that chokes him.

meaning: The gusset is the extra piece in the crotch of the fundoshi. The first time you see it, the esteem-part is above the rice field, and the crown sits on top, but the mouth is the opening where the gusset fits.
reading: トウ — A 'toe' (トウ) pokes through the gusset hole in the fundoshi, and you see it sticking out from the rice field.

meaning: A short coat that you buy for the first time. The wrapping enclosure holds the insect, and the buy-part is on the side, but the coat is so short it only covers the insect's back.
reading: ショク — 'Shock' (ショク) — you get a shock when you see the price of this short coat, and the insect on it bites you.

meaning: To strip bare — you take off the garment and lay it on the ground. The first time you do it, the one-stroke and lid are on top, the box is empty, and the day is bright, so you see the naked body.
reading: タン — A 'tan' (a sun-tan) — you strip bare to get a tan, and the day (日) is hot, so you lay on the box to dry.

meaning: On a dish, a retainer's first time — he sees two ragged cloths and the 乞-shaped part, all torn into rags.
reading: ラン — The retainer runs (ラン) through the rags, tripping and tearing them more.

meaning: Rain (雨) falls on a garment (衣) but 'and yet' (而) the first time (初) you wear it, it's underwear — so it stays dry because it's hidden under everything else.
reading: ジュ — Underwear is 'ju'st for you — say 'ju' as in 'just' when you slip into your private layer.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a sweeping stroke (ノ) on top, and below it a first time (初) you buy (買) with a halberd (戈) — you use the halberd to cut the grass (艾) to stuff into your socks, which are part of the garment.
reading: ベツ — Socks are 'bet'ter than bare feet — say 'bets' as in 'bets on' wearing them to keep warm.

meaning: A large day with white sun — the first time you see it, you need a raincoat to stay dry.
reading: セキ — The raincoat is so thick it feels like a 'セキ' (seki) — a heavy stone — on your shoulders.

meaning: A shellfish with an eye and two splayed strokes, a mouth, soil, and a page — all tucked into your obi for the first time.
reading: ケツ — You tuck the page into your obi with a 'ケツ' (ketsu) — a quick kick of your hip to secure it.

meaning: A vertical stroke, a dot, a sweeping stroke, two, day, water — all on the first time — that's the collar you expose to the rain.
reading: ハク — You expose your collar and shout 'ハク' (haku) — like a hawk's cry — to show you're not afraid.

meaning: A first time (初) you see (見) a tree (木) standing up (立) — but it's not a tree, it's a person in underwear, the thin layer hidden under clothes.
reading: The underwear is so thin you can "sheen" (シン) through it — a shiny sheen of fabric in the light.

meaning: A garment (衣) with a month (月) and a stand (立) under a lid (亠) — the enemy attacks, advancing on you, piling up like layers of clothing, and you must succeed to the next position to escape.
reading: シュウ — The attack comes like a "shoe" (シュウ) thrown at you — a garment (衣) flies, a month (月) passes, and you stand (立) up to fend off the pile of shoes attacking you.

meaning: The gate is open, and a day's worth of cloth is draped over a tree, with the first time you see it you think of a special kind of fabric used for robes.
reading: ラン — A lantern (ラン) hangs by the gate, its light shining on the cloth draped over the tree.

meaning: A first time (初) you wear a skirt with a pleat (襵) — the ear (耳) hears the rustle of the pleat as you move, and you fold it like a first-time tailor.
reading: The pleat in the skirt makes a 'sho' (ショウ) sound — like a 'show' of pleats, as if the skirt is on a runway, and the pleats are the star of the show.

meaning: Your hand holds a cord that ties up your sleeves, and the cord is marked with two short strokes on top, showing it's a special loop, while the esteem of the gesture makes it a kokuji.
reading: タスキ — The cord is a 'tasuk' (タスキ) you tie, like a sash, to hold your sleeves up.

meaning: A large hand mixes with a tree, and the first time you see this loop, it's a belt band that wraps around the tree trunk.
reading: The loop is a 'han' (ハン) — like a hangman's noose, but for your belt.

meaning: A dot, two, legs, splayed strokes, katakana-mu, nine, soil, and grass on top all hang from the first time — but the sleeve is what you wave, and the grass brushes it.
reading: The sleeve flutters as you say 'gey' (ゲイ) — like a gay parade waving long sleeves.

meaning: West is a cover — picture the sun setting in the west, and a giant lid (the west radical) slamming down on top of the land to cover it for night.
reading: The cover goes 'ah' as it drops — say 'AH' while placing a lid on a box, like the west radical doing its job.

meaning: The sun sets in the west, and the shape of the kanji looks like a setting sun with a line through it — but you can also see it as a mountain (山) under an upside-down box (冂) with a one (一) on top, all pointing to the west horizon.
reading: The west wind blows 'sei' (セイ) — say 'say' as you point west, 'say west'.

meaning: This is just the upside-down box with a lid and a vertical stroke — it's the bare skeleton of radical 146, nothing more.
reading: No reading needed — it's a variant, so just see it as a 'west' (西) without the inner bits, a ghost of a radical.

meaning: A woman (女) stands to the west (西) — she is the main point, the essence you need, the pivot around which everything turns.
reading: YŌ — Say 'yo!' to the woman in the west — she's the one you need, the essential pivot of your whole plan.

meaning: Ten west-facing days stretch out deep and large, like a long shadow extending across the land under the sun.
reading: The deep, large shadow extends like a 'tan' (タン) — a tan line that spreads over your skin after many days in the sun.

meaning: A stooping figure (夂) leans over from the west (西), casting a shade over the day (日) below, while a stop (彳) and the 乞-shaped part (乞) cling to the side — together they capsize the whole scene, covering it like a mantle.
reading: Imagine a huge フク (fuku) — a giant pufferfish — that capsizes a boat and then covers the wreckage with its spiky shade, hiding it from the day.

meaning: Leather (革) wraps a month (月) and west (西) — imagine a leather belt cinching the west, claiming supremacy over all lands, making you the champion.
reading: The champion's roar 'ハ' sounds like a sharp 'HA!' as he strikes a winning pose.

meaning: You investigate (覈) by looking west (西) at a white (白) direction (方) sign, then strike (攵) it with the 乞-shaped part (乞) to see if it's true — a thorough check.
reading: カク — You 'crack' the case open to investigate — 'kaku' sounds like 'crack' when you break through the mystery.

meaning: Reins are made of leather (革) and connect to a horse (馬) — the reins are tied with a short thread (幺) and thread (糸), with west (西) and four dots (杰) showing the horse's direction.
reading: The sound is キ — picture a key (キ) that unlocks the reins, letting the horse run free.

meaning: An eye (目) on top of a pair of legs (儿) — you see with your eye while your legs carry you toward what you hope to see.
reading: ケン — Imagine a KEN doll standing on a stage, using his eye to scan the audience for chances and hopes.

meaning: A person (人) with two (二) eyes sees (見) a large (大) soil (土) mound — this is the standard measure, the ruler you use to measure the mound's size.
reading: The person measures the soil with a 'KI' (like 'key') — the key is the standard tool for unlocking the correct measurement.

meaning: A 'pair of legs' (儿) under an 'eye' (目) that 'sees' (見) — when you wake from sleep, your legs move and your eyes open, and you 'realize' (to realize) where you are. The 'to mix with' (爻) suggests thoughts blending in as you wake.
reading: When you wake up, you go 'kaku' (カク) — like a rooster's 'cock-a-doodle-doo' but shortened to 'kaku' as you realize it's morning.

meaning: A 'claw' (爪) reaching out from above an 'eye' (見) — you claw at your eye to see better while searching (seek) for something lost on the ground.
reading: To 'seek' is to 'ベキ' (ベキ) — imagine saying 'Beki, beki!' like a chicken pecking and searching for seeds, each peck a 'beki' sound.

meaning: A 'one' (一) with a 'vertical stroke' (｜) and a 'dot' (丶) and a 'sweeping stroke' (ノ) all crowd around an 'eye' (目) that 'sees' (見) — you search (to search for) by scanning every tiny detail, even a dot or a stroke, with your eye.
reading: Searching hard, you mutter 'ベキ' (ベキ) — like 'beki' as in 'I beki (better) find it!' — a quick, determined sound.

meaning: You 'see' with your eyes, but here the 'salute' radical stands beside 'see' — you salute what you inspect, like a guard checking a badge with a formal look.
reading: シ — Say 'she' — you see her, and you salute her as she inspects the parade.

meaning: You see through a mouth-shaped hole with a barb and one line — you peep in, and the scene comes in sight.
reading: You 'shee' (シ) — like 'she' — peeping through the hole, whispering 'she's there!'

meaning: You see through a mouth with a divining rod — you peek to divine what's hidden, a quick glance to check the omens.
reading: You 'ten' (テン) — like 'tent' — peek through the tent flap to see who's outside.

meaning: A crown sits on top of an esteem-worthy head, but the eyes (see) are wide open — you're memorizing by keeping watch, not just nodding off. The crown is the 冖, the esteem is the 尚, and the see is the 見 — together they show a wakeful, learning mind.
reading: カク — Imagine a loud "cackle" (カク) from a rooster that wakes you up — you memorize the sound because the rooster's call forces you to remember the morning.

meaning: A dot, a sweeping stroke, a pair of legs, ice, an eye, and see — on a mission, you must see through the ice with your eye, using your legs to walk the path.
reading: You go on a 'チョウ' (chou) mission — like 'chow' — and you're so hungry you can only see food, not the enemy.

meaning: A craft (工) person (人) who can see (見) spirits — that’s the diviner or medium.
reading: ゲキ — “Geck” like a gecko — the medium sees a gecko spirit on the wall.

meaning: A vertical stroke (｜) and a pair of legs (儿) under a lid (一) with two splayed strokes (ハ) — this is a person who hides their day (日) and eye (目) because they can't see (見) you, feeling ashamed.
reading: The 'テン' sound is like 'ten' — imagine being so ashamed you can only count to ten before hiding your face.

meaning: To covet high rank, you reap the month's harvest with your eye — you see the hat on top and want it for yourself.
reading: You 'yu' (you) want that throne — it's all about you, your ambition. (ユ)

meaning: A retainer (臣) with two (二) lines and the 乞-shaped part (乞) looks through a see (見) — he is perusing a document, scanning every line carefully.
reading: ラン — Imagine a 'ran' (run) through a museum — you quickly peruse each exhibit, but you see everything in a blur.

meaning: To see, you use your eye on the day — the old man's ten fingers point at what's visible, right in front of you.
reading: You 'to' (toe) the line to get a better view — step up on your toes to see. (ト)

meaning: A parent stands under a lid, watching their child with a spicy expression — the intimacy of family is built on seeing and enduring. The two short strokes on top (并) sit above the tree, but the core is the eye (目) of the parent who sees everything.
reading: シン — Imagine a parent saying 'shin' as they shin up a tree to check on their kid, the spicy (辛) tree bark making them wince.

meaning: A mountain of beans sits under a see, with a mouth and two short strokes on top — you're so hungry for rank you'd climb that bean-mountain just to peek over the top at the throne.
reading: The sound is 'ki' — think of a key (ki) that unlocks the door to the high-ranking office, but you're still coveting it from outside.

meaning: An upside-down box with a one inside, and a see peeking out — you happen to meet someone by looking through that box's opening.
reading: The sound is 'kou' — imagine you 'kow' (like a cow's moo, 'kō') as you bump into an old friend on the street — a happy, surprised meeting.

meaning: To spy, you watch for someone from behind a tiger. The tiger spots are on the cliff, and the eye is on the spoon, but the divining rod and the pair of legs are hidden — you peek with the see-part.
reading: ソ — 'So' (ソ) — you say 'so...' quietly as you spy, using the eye and the see-part to watch for the tiger's prey.

meaning: A gentleman (士) with a see (見) eye stands on soil (土) under grass on top (艾), while a mouth (口) and two (二) witnesses gather — you have an audience with the emperor, so you see him clearly.
reading: キン — Imagine a king (キン) granting you an audience, and you must see him while kneeling on a golden cushion.

meaning: An old bird (隹) with a dart (矢) in its beak, and the 乞-shaped part (乞) as its eye — you see (見) this strange sight, so you take an outlook on it.
reading: カン — You KAN (can) see the whole view from the top of a hill — the outlook is so clear you say "I can see everything!"

meaning: You steal a look through a gate (門) at a pair of legs (儿) and a month (月) — you see (見) an eye (目) peeping at you, so you spy back through the gate.
reading: カン — You 'can' peek through the gate — 'kan' sounds like 'can' as in 'I can see you' when you spy.

meaning: A pair of legs (儿) stands under an upside-down box (冂) that holds a マ-shaped stroke (マ) and a claw (爪) over an eye (目) — but the eye is also a see (見) part. You look about in a complicated order, trying to see what’s inside the box, but the sequence of parts is so tangled you can’t express it.
reading: The reading is ラ. Imagine a 'ラ' (ra) sound like 'rah' — you look about and say 'Rah! What a mess of parts!' — the complicated thought is a loud 'rah' of confusion.

meaning: A tiger spots (虍) a cliff (厂) where a spoon (匕) and a divining rod (卜) lie. You peep at them through an eye (目) that is also a see (見) part — you watch and spy on the scene from behind the cliff, careful not to be seen.
reading: The reading is ソ. Imagine 'so' — you spy on someone and whisper 'so... so...' as you peep, like a sneaky 'so' sound.

meaning: In a mortar, you see a crown and to mix with — but you must memorize the sight before it fades.
reading: カク — You memorize by saying 'カク' (kaku) — like a quick 'cack' of a hen — to lock it in your brain.

meaning: An upside-down box (冂) with two splayed strokes (ハ) and a vertical stroke (｜) holds a pair of legs (儿) and an eye (目) that sees (見) — you mix (爻) all the details with one (一) look to explain everything in detail.
reading: You explain every detail with a "rah" (ラ) — like a cheerleader's rah, but you're laying out the whole story step by step.

meaning: A retainer buys a shellfish with his eyes, but he also sees a pair of legs and a box, so he must look at it all carefully to inspect and perceive.
reading: ラン — A lantern (ラン) lights the scene as the retainer looks at the shellfish to inspect it.

meaning: A gentleman with a pair of legs stands in a box, and he sees a shellfish with an eye, so he meets and sees you face to face.
reading: テキ — A tech (テキ) guy meets you, and you see his face clearly.

meaning: An old bird with a mouth and ten eyes sees everything — the outlook and appearance you get from this all-seeing view.
reading: You 'can' (カン) see everything with this outlook — like a can of eyes.

meaning: A wrapping enclosure wraps around a month, but a vertical stroke pokes out from the top — like a horn or a corner of a box that juts out.
reading: カク — Imagine a cow's horn getting stuck in a cactus, and the cow says "KAH-ku!" (like "cactus" without the 'tus').

meaning: A vertical stroke (｜) of power (力) inside a wrapping enclosure (勹) — the catty (觔) is a unit of weight, like a bundle of muscle (月) and sinew (角) wrapped tight.
reading: The catty (觔) weighs a 'kin' (キン) — imagine a golden 'kin' (キン) bar balanced on a scale, exactly one catty.

meaning: A 'cow' (牛) with an 'angle' (角) — but the 'wrapping enclosure' (勹) and 'month' (月) are rough and unfinished. The cow's horn is coarse (coarse) and rude, not smooth — the 'vertical stroke' (｜) pokes out like a rough edge.
reading: The cow's horn is 'ソ' (ソ) — imagine saying 'so-so' (ソソ) as you feel its rough, coarse texture, not smooth at all.

meaning: A 'person' (人) with a 'ユ-shaped stroke' (ユ) and a 'wrapping enclosure' (勹) around a 'month' (月) — but the 'angle' (角) is broken. The person longs (to long for) for a full month, but the angle is cut off, leaving them dissatisfied (dissatisfied).
reading: Longing for something, you sigh 'ケツ' (ケツ) — like 'ketsu' as in 'ketsu (get it?)' — but you don't get it, so you're dissatisfied.

meaning: A melon and an angle — this cup is shaped like a melon cut at an angle, with a sharp corner for a handle.
reading: You drink from this cup and say 'コ' (ko) — like 'caw' of a crow, but you're sipping melon juice.

meaning: The angle of a stop sign has a spoon stuck in it, and the spoon is shaped like a bird's beak — so this is a beak, or bill.
reading: The beak of a bird goes 'shi-shu' as it pecks — imagine a sparrow saying 'shi' while it pecks at a spoon.

meaning: An angle of a family name collides with you — you feel the touch of a horn, a conflict with a relative's stubborn pride.
reading: You 'tei' (テイ) — like 'tie' — feel the collision as a tie pulls tight around your neck, a conflict you can't escape.

meaning: An angle (角) of a cow (牛) is cut with a sword (刀) to unravel the knot — the key to the puzzle is in the cut.
reading: Unravel the mystery with KAI (カイ) — imagine a kayak (kai) paddling through a tangled rope, slicing it apart to find the answer.

meaning: A cup made of horn (the angle of a horn) is decorated with a vertical stroke, a pair of legs, a wrapping enclosure, and the esteem of the month — it's an obstinate, fancy drinking cup.
reading: The horn cup is so big you say 'ko-u' as you lift it — like 'cow' but with a long 'o' — imagine a cow's horn cup.

meaning: An angle (角) of an insect (虫) touches you — you feel its hard shell and jump back.
reading: The insect's feeler gives a 'SHOKU' (ショク) — a sharp electric touch that makes you flinch.

meaning: A king's angle is crossed with two short strokes on top of a sheep — this unlocks the notes and key to understanding, like solving a puzzle.
reading: You 'kai' the lock of understanding — imagine a key turning with a click that sounds like 'kai'.

meaning: An angle (角) with a wrapping enclosure (勹) around a month (月) and water (水) — the curve is strong, bending like a bow (the 勹 is the bow, the 角 is the horn).
reading: キュウ — “Q” like a strong “cue” — a strong cue stick bends but doesn’t break.

meaning: An angle (角) with a wrapping enclosure (勹) around a mouth (口) and a tree (木) — the tree trembles with fear when the mouth screams inside the enclosure.
reading: ソク — “Sock” — you tremble with fear when someone throws a sock at you.

meaning: An angle (角) with a barb (亅) on one side and a wrapping enclosure (勹) on the other, plus a large (大) mouth (口) and a month (月) — the horns of an ox: one turns up, the other turns down.
reading: Imagine a horn that turns up and one that turns down, like a key (キー) in a lock — the sound is 'ki' as in 'key'.

meaning: A tartar horn is a chilly wind that blows from a cliff — the wrapping enclosure holds the mouth, and the halberd's angle cuts through the month's cold air.
reading: The wind is so cold it makes you 'hitsu' (hiss) — a sharp, icy breath. (ヒツ)

meaning: A pike (殳) strikes an angle (角) that sits under a crown (冖) with a table (几) and a wrapping enclosure (勹) — the goblet is knocked over, spilling the ancient measure, and you're frightened by the clatter.
reading: The sound is 'koku' — think of a 'cock' (koku) crowing loudly, startling you so much you drop your goblet in fright.

meaning: A sweeping stroke (ノ) cuts an angle (角) into a day (日) that is not (勿) a one (一) — the wrapping enclosure (勹) holds the 乞-shaped part (乞) like a cup for drinking.
reading: ショウ — The cup is so big you shout 'SHOW!' (ショウ) as you lift it to toast.

meaning: An angle (角) is wrapped in a wrapping enclosure (勹) that holds a ten (十) and a mouth (口) — but the mouth is also a day (日) and a month (月) inside a rice field (田). This horn goblet is a strange container: the angle is the horn, and the wrapping holds the drink, like a ritual cup for a feast.
reading: The reading is シ. Imagine 'she' — a lady named 'She' raises a horn goblet and says 'She drinks from this 觶.' The sound 'shi' is in 'she'.

meaning: An angle (角) of a horn touches an insect (虫), and then you buy (買) a wrapping enclosure (勹) to protect it — the horn's tip feels the insect, so you touch it.
reading: ショク — Imagine a 'SHOCK' (ショク) of electricity when you touch the insect's horn — you feel a jolt.

meaning: An old bird (隹) pecks at a mountain (山) inside an upside-down box (冂), while a pair of legs (儿) dangle from a wrapping enclosure (勹) — all carved into a sharp ivory bodkin that also has an angle (角) and a month (月) symbol on it.
reading: ケイ — Imagine a cake (ケイ) being pierced by this ivory bodkin, the horn tip poking through the frosting.

meaning: A lid (亠) over a mouth (not listed, but the shape is like a tongue) — what comes out from under the lid is your word, what you say.
reading: ゲン — Picture a GENIE (ゲン) popping out of a bottle, and every word it says comes true.

meaning: A say (言) with a barb (亅) and one (一) line — you correct the text by adding a barb-like mark to revise it.
reading: You 'tei' (テイ) the mistake — like 'tay' in 'taylor' — you tailor the words to fix them.

meaning: A divining rod (卜) is placed on a say (言) — the rod points to the news of death, an obituary announcement.
reading: フ — The obituary says 'FOO' (フ) — a short, solemn sound like a funeral bell tolling once.

meaning: A wrapping enclosure (勹) around the say (言) — the sound of a crash (訇) is like a loud 'boom' that wraps around your words, silencing them.
reading: The crash (訇) goes 'kou' (コウ) — imagine a giant 'kou' (コウ) bell crashing down, making a deafening sound.

meaning: The say part on the left is speaking out loud, while the ten on the right stands for a complete set of ten steps. Together, they suggest someone talking through a ten-step plan or scheme.
reading: ケイ — Imagine a detective saying 'ケイ' (like 'kay') as he plots a plan, tapping his chin with a pencil, saying 'Kay, here's the scheme.'

meaning: To request and question: you say (言) something to a person sitting at a table (几) — you ask them a question, and they lean forward to investigate your words.
reading: The question is 'jin' (ジン) — like 'gin' — you ask for a gin and tonic, but the bartender investigates your ID first.

meaning: To get confused: you say (言) something, but the craft (工) of your words is all tangled — like a worker mixing up tools, your speech becomes a mess.
reading: The confusion is 'kou' (コウ) — like 'cow' — a cow gets confused and moos loudly, but you can't understand what it's saying.

meaning: Say (言) something, then use a measurement (寸) — you chastise and attack with words, measuring your blows to defeat the enemy.
reading: トウ — You 'tow' (トウ) the enemy away after attacking, dragging them off the battlefield.

meaning: A barb and two lines cross over the say part, stretching it wide — this is a boast that exaggerates everything into something great and broad.
reading: The boastful guy says 'ク' (coo) like a pigeon puffing its chest out wide.

meaning: A dry stick pokes the say part, forcing it to spill secrets — this is divulging or revealing what was hidden.
reading: The reveal comes with a sharp 'ケツ' (ketsu) — like a kick that knocks the truth out.

meaning: A vertical stroke, a hook stroke, a spoon, and the classical 'to be' all twist around the say part — this is a deceitful, arrogant tangle of words.
reading: The cheat says 'シ' (shi) — like 'she' who lies with a sly smile.

meaning: A sweeping stroke and a sword cut into the say part, making it hesitate — this is being reluctant to speak.
reading: The hesitation sounds like 'ジン' (jin) — as in 'jinx', when you can't get the words out.

meaning: Say (言) a stream (川) of words — that's instruction, explaining how to read a character in Japanese.
reading: クン — Think of a COON (raccoon) sitting in class, listening to the teacher's instruction, nodding its masked head.

meaning: A mountain sits on the say part, crushing it — this is abuse and slander that ridicules from a high peak.
reading: The slander comes with a 'サン' (san) — like 'sun' burning down harshly on the victim.

meaning: A hook stroke and the 乞-shaped part grab the say part and pull it to a stop — this is coming to an end, finally arriving.
reading: The end arrives with a 'キツ' (kitsu) — like 'kits' (young foxes) finally settling down after a long run.

meaning: You take a hook stroke (乙) and a say (言) — you hook someone's words and hang them on a one (一) — that's how you consign a request to them. The top part (ノ, 一, 乙) is like a hook you hang your message on.
reading: You 'TAKU' a package to a courier — the word 'TAKU' sounds like 'tackle' — you tackle someone to hand them your task.

meaning: A say on the left, and a stop on the right — you say something and then stop, writing it down as a scribe's account or narrative.
reading: The scribe writes with a 'KEY' (sounds like 'ki') — he uses a key to unlock the story.

meaning: A person at the side (化) is speaking (言) with a spoon (匕) in their mouth, so their words come out twisted — that's an accent or dialect.
reading: A cat (カ) tries to say 'meow' but a spoon (匕) in its mouth makes it come out as a strange dialect — 'ka' is the cat's mangled sound.

meaning: A tusk (牙) is stuck in your say (言) — you try to speak but the tusk blocks your words, so you look at the speaker with doubt.
reading: The tusk (牙) makes you go 'GAH!' in doubt — the sound of a sharp surprise.

meaning: The say part on the left is a mouth speaking, while the two splayed strokes on top of the katakana-mu shape on the right look like two people pointing fingers at each other. This is a public accusation — you sue someone by saying your case loudly while both sides gesture.
reading: ショウ — Imagine a judge in court shouting 'SHOW me the evidence!' as you sue someone. The word 'show' sounds like ショウ.

meaning: A vertical stroke (｜) shoots up from a bow (弓) while someone says (言) 'even more' — the arrow goes much further, still more than before.
reading: Shin (シン) is the sound of a bowstring twanging as it shoots an arrow that goes much more (訠) — 'shin' like the twang.

meaning: A person says (言) with a bow (弓) drawn — the bow creaks and the person chants and moans in rhythm with the tension.
reading: No reading given, so use the kun-like image: 'gin' (as in a moan) — but since no reading is listed, skip this one.

meaning: An axe (斤) chops wood, and the person says (言) 'yay!' — they are pleased and delighted with the clean cut.
reading: Kin (キン) — imagine a happy lumberjack shouting 'Kin!' as the axe (斤) splits the log, delighted (訢) with the result.

meaning: A person (人) says (言) goodbye with a large (大) wave, but a two (二) and a ユ-shaped stroke (ユ) show the secret parting — the secret of separation.
reading: Ketsu (ケツ) — 'ketsu' sounds like 'get you' — as they part, one says 'I'll get you later' — that's the secret (訣) of their separation.

meaning: A person (人) inside an upside-down box (冂) tries to say (言) something, but the box muffles it — they stutter and can't get the words out.
reading: Totsu (トツ) — 'totsu' sounds like 'tots' — a stuttering person says 't-t-tots' while stuck in the box (冂), unable to speak clearly.

meaning: A say part stands on a hook stroke, while a crown sits above crooked-big — the sincere person speaks with a steady, faithful heart, not a crooked one.
reading: The sound is 'shin' — imagine a sincere monk saying 'shin' as he bows, his voice steady and true.

meaning: You 'say' something, then you move in a 'direction' — that's how you visit: you speak your intention and walk toward the person's home.
reading: ホウ — Imagine 'hoe' — you visit a farmer, and he hands you a hoe to help in the field while you chat.

meaning: A say part is crowded by little strokes and a sweeping stroke — the clamour of many small voices rising into an uproar.
reading: The sound is 'sou' — imagine a loud crowd shouting 'SOU!' in annoyance at a noisy street performer.

meaning: You say (言) with your right hand (又) holding a pike (殳) on a table (几) — you prepare an establishment for a meeting.
reading: You SET up the table and pike — 'SET-su' the scene for the new office.

meaning: A person says (言) "ten" (十) and the 乞-shaped part (乞) — like a hand reaching out — so you permit them to take it. The dry (干) strokes above are the stamp of approval.
reading: キョ — Picture a strict teacher saying "KYO!" (like "key-oh") as she permits you to enter the classroom.

meaning: The say (言) part is a flag (尸) with a dot (丶) on top — you translate the flag's message. The reason and circumstance are hidden in the dot, so you must explain the case.
reading: You translate a mysterious note and say 'ya-ku' (ヤク) — like a yak chewing slowly while you figure out the meaning.

meaning: An axe (斤) cuts a say (言) with a dot (丶) — imagine someone using an axe to chop a speech bubble, then a dot (period) falls, making the accusation final. You sue, complaining of pain.
reading: You bring the accusation to court and say 'SO' (ソ) — like 'so?' as in 'so what do you have to say for yourself?' — a sharp, short sound.

meaning: A mouth (口) with a barb (亅) and a one (一) — the barb pokes out of the mouth as it says (言) harsh words, scolding you.
reading: The scold says 'KA!' like a sharp command — 'KA, stop that!'

meaning: A doctor uses a 'say' (言) to examine you, while a 'hat on top' (个) sits over your head and 'three' (彡) lines on the chart show your pulse — that's a checkup.
reading: シン — Imagine a doctor saying 'SHIN' as he shines a light into your eyes during the exam.

meaning: A king (王) puts a dot (丶) on his say (言) — the dot marks a special note, a comment for the king's words.
reading: The king's note says 'CHUU!' — like a little 'choo' of a train, a quick comment.

meaning: One (一) line of say (言) stops (止) at a point — that's the evidence that proves the certificate.
reading: ショウ — Picture a show where the witness holds up a certificate, saying 'Show this proof!'

meaning: A wrapping enclosure (勹) holds a mouth (口) that says (言) — the mouth is trapped and blames you, shouting from inside the wrap.
reading: The blame comes as a low 'KOU' — like a groan of 'koh' from the trapped mouth.

meaning: A spoon (匕) stops (止) your say (言) — the spoon blocks your words, so you can only bad-mouth and criticize from behind.
reading: The spoon stops you with a 'SHI' — like a hiss of 'shh' before you speak.

meaning: A divining rod (卜) pokes a mouth (口) that says (言) — the rod makes the mouth chatter and whisper, garrulous and joking.
reading: The rod makes you 'TAN' — like a quick 'tan-tan' tap, a playful whisper.

meaning: A 'say' (言) part sits above a 'mouth' (口) and 'ten' (十) — imagine a scholar with ten mouths explaining ancient texts, each mouth giving a different interpretation. This is exegesis: critical analysis of classical writings.
reading: コ — A 'コ' (ko) sound like 'co-' in 'codex', the ancient manuscript you're analyzing line by line.

meaning: A 'say' (言) part with a 'hat on top' (个) and a 'マ-shaped stroke' (マ) — picture a street vendor wearing a hat, shouting 'マ' to attract buyers, while a 'barb' (亅) and 'one' (一) hang from his stall. He's selling his wares.
reading: レイ — 'レイ' sounds like 'lay' — imagine laying out goods on a mat to sell them.

meaning: The 'say' part on the left is speaking, and the 'family name' part on the right is the target — you use your words to vilify or denounce someone's family name, dragging it through the mud.
reading: For テイ, think of a 'tay' (like the English word 'tay' as in 'tea' but said with a hard T) — you 'tay' (denounce) someone's name with a sharp 'テイ' sound, like a spit of contempt.

meaning: A 'say' (言) part above a 'buy' (買) — picture a customer buying something, then the seller 'says' (言) something so ridiculous the customer starts to ridicule them. The 'buy' (買) is the trigger for the mockery.
reading: リ — 'リ' sounds like 'lee' — imagine a crowd 'lee' (laughing) at a ridiculous purchase, ridiculing the buyer.

meaning: A 'box-on-side enclosure' (匚) with a 'mouth' (口) inside, and a 'say' (言) on top — imagine a box that suddenly opens its mouth and says something shocking, making you exclaim in surprise. This is an interjection of astonishment.
reading: キョ — 'キョ' sounds like 'kyo' in 'kyoto' — imagine visiting Kyoto and being surprised by a talking box that says 'Kyo!'

meaning: A vertical stroke and a sweeping stroke lean on the say part, twisting its words into a lie — the falsehood is in how the strokes bend the speech.
reading: サ — Imagine a liar saying 'SAH-ry, I didn't do it!' with a fake, theatrical sigh, the sound 'sa' dripping from their mouth.

meaning: A 'say' (言) part with a 'roof' (宀) and a 'spoon' (匕) — picture someone under a roof, using a spoon to stir a pot of lies, 'saying' (言) sweet words to deceive you. This is to deceive or delude.
reading: イ — 'イ' sounds like 'ee' in 'eel' — imagine a slippery eel under a roof, deceiving you with its smooth talk.

meaning: A mouth (口) inside a say (言) box, with a katakana-mu shape (厶) sitting on top like a sneaky hat — the whole thing is a trickster's tool, so it means to deceive or cheat, and also to give something away (leave behind) as a trap.
reading: The sneaky hat (厶) says 'I' (イ) as it slips a lie into your mouth — the reading is イ.

meaning: The say-mouth speaks with a sword's edge — that's an imperial edict, a command from the throne.
reading: The edict is read aloud with a 'SHO' of trumpets, like 'show' of royal power.

meaning: A vertical stroke (｜) and one (一) stand on two (二) short strokes (并) while a person says (言) something—this is how you evaluate and comment on their words.
reading: ヒョウ — A 'hyo' (ヒョウ) is a leopard, and you criticize its spots as you evaluate its coat.

meaning: A biased argument is like a branch (支) that has been bent to one side by a right hand (又) under a cliff (厂), while the say (言) part shows it's all about words — the words lean one way, not both.
reading: ヒ — Picture a biased referee blowing a whistle that sounds like 'hee' as he points only to one side, ignoring the other team's protests.

meaning: A say (言) box with an upside-down box (冂) on top and a mouth (口) inside — you peek through the box's opening to spy on what the mouth says, so it means to spy upon or give information, and being shrewd means you notice everything.
reading: The spy peeks through the upside-down box (冂) and whispers 'kyo' (キョウ) — the reading is キョウ.

meaning: A say (言) box with a vertical stroke (｜) poking down into an open box enclosure (凵) — the stroke bends and stoops as it enters the box, so it means to bend, stoop, crouch, or yield.
reading: The bent stroke (｜) curls into the open box (凵) and says 'kutsu' (クツ) like a crouching cat — the reading is クツ.

meaning: A say (言) box with an eye (目) inside — you speak words while staring with a hateful eye, so it means to curse.
reading: The eye (目) in the say box glares and hisses 'so' (ソ) like a snake's curse — the reading is ソ.

meaning: A mouth (口) speaks words, and a barb (亅) pierces the one (一) truth — but the say (言) part shows these are just parts of speech, not full sentences. The mouth shapes the words, the barb marks the poetic twist.
reading: シ — Think of a 'she' (シ) who writes poetry, her words flowing like a river of 'she' verses. Every poem she writes is a 'she' poem.

meaning: Your say (言) flows like water (水) with a dot (丶) on top — that’s a poem or song you recite aloud.
reading: You recite a poem about a “ei” (like “ay” in “say”) — the sound echoes off the water.

meaning: A sweeping stroke of ice on feathers, and you say (say) it — that's boasting, bragging, making yourself well known.
reading: The boastful bird says 'ku' — like a crow's 'caw' but short — imagine a crow bragging with a 'ku'.

meaning: You say (say) to the day, wrapped in a wrapping enclosure — that's consulting with someone, asking for their opinion.
reading: You 'jun' to consult — imagine a judge (sounds like 'jun') asking you questions in court.

meaning: You say (say) to the day, and a spoon is there — you visit a temple, arrive, and attain enlightenment.
reading: You 'kei' to the temple — imagine saying 'kei' as you bow at the gate, like 'kay' but with a long 'e'.

meaning: You say (言) something, then use a craft (工) and a piling (弋) to build a test — you try it out.
reading: You 'shee' (シ) — like a quiet 'shh' — as you carefully try the craft's new tool.

meaning: A dot (丶) sits on top of an evening (夕) scene, while a say (言) box below records what is found — you examine into the case judicially, uncovering the truth.
reading: サツ — Imagine a judge in a courtroom saying 'SATS!' as he slams his gavel, examining the evidence laid out before him.

meaning: The say part on the left is talking, and on the right the measurement and soil parts form a temple where poems are recited. So, poetry is what is said at a sacred ceremony.
reading: The sound is 'shi' — imagine a poet reciting a verse while holding a sheet of paper that says 'SHI' in big letters, and the audience whispers 'shi, shi' in approval.

meaning: A sweeping stroke (ノ) and a hook stroke (乙) under a roof (宀) with say (言) — you say words under a roof to apologize.
reading: You say 'ta' (タ) — 'ta' like 'tah' as in 'tah, I'm sorry' — a short apologetic sound.

meaning: The say part on the left is speaking harsh words, while the right side shows a mouth under a cliff — imagine someone standing under a cliff shouting insults up at you, and the cliff echoes the ridicule back down.
reading: The sound is コウ — think of a "koala" clinging to the cliff, screeching insults at you from above, its voice echoing as コウ.

meaning: A say (言) word is wrapped in a wrapping enclosure (勹) with a seal (卩) and a cliff (厂) — the hidden, twisted message is a lie to deceive you.
reading: キ — Think of a 'key' (キ) that unlocks a secret door, but behind it is a liar who deceives you with false words.

meaning: A king (王) puts a hat on top (个) of a say (言) box, with two splayed strokes (ハ) underneath — he discusses methods and selects the best result.
reading: セン — Imagine a 'sen' (セン) senator in a debate, discussing and selecting the best course of action.

meaning: A gentleman (士) opens his mouth (口) to speak, but the say (言) part is packed so tight that the words come out pressed and close together — you reprove him for being so cramped.
reading: キツ — Picture a box so packed (詰) that when you try to close it, it goes 'KITS!' (キツ) like a tight squeeze.

meaning: A say-mouth speaks with a tongue — the tale is told, the talk flows from the mouth.
reading: The tongue says 'WA' (wah) as it wags in the mouth — that's the talk.

meaning: The say (言) part is under a lid (亠), with a person (人) and a sweeping stroke (ノ) plus a dot (丶) — this specific word is the one we said before, the above-stated one.
reading: When you say 'that specific one,' you point and say 'ガイ' (gai) — like 'guy' — 'that guy over there.'

meaning: The sheep (羊) stands next to the say (言) part, and the two short strokes on top (并) are like tiny notes. The sheep is giving a detailed, accurate report — every little stroke counts.
reading: The sheep (羊) is so detailed it even knows the show (ショウ) times of every barn dance. Imagine the sheep reciting a full schedule.

meaning: A say (言) word is placed on soil (土) with a one (一) and a sweeping stroke (ノ) above, and a pair of legs (儿) below — many people come to inquire and question.
reading: シン — Picture a 'shin' (シン) guard asking numerous questions at the gate, inquiring about everyone who passes.

meaning: A pair of legs (儿) stand under two splayed strokes (ハ) and a wrapping enclosure (勹) on a cliff (厂), while a say (言) box chatters — this person talks too much, verbose.
reading: セン — Think of a 'sen' (セン)ior citizen who talks too much, rambling on and on about his surname and family history.

meaning: A stooping figure (夂) leans over a mouth (口) to shout orders, while the say (言) radical on the side shows these are spoken commands.
reading: ガク — Imagine a strict general shouting orders: 'GACK!' — the sound of a command so sharp it makes you gack like a cough.

meaning: A cliff (厂) has a fire (火) burning at its base, and someone says (言) a jest to distract from the danger — the joke is the spark of wit.
reading: カイ — Picture a comedian on a cliff (厂) with a fire (火) saying (言) a joke that makes the crowd shout 'KAI!' like a cheer.

meaning: A wrapping enclosure (勹) holds a dot (丶) and a sweeping stroke (ノ) inside an open box (凵), all jumbled together, while say (言) adds the noise — it's a chaotic, uproarious mess.
reading: キョウ — Imagine a noisy crowd shouting 'KYO!' as they tumble out of an open box (凵) — the sound of uproar.

meaning: Soil (土) is piled over a say (言) — words buried in dirt, leading to error and deception because the truth is hidden.
reading: カイ — A mistake that makes you slap your forehead and say 'KAI!' — like 'kai' in 'kayak' capsized, a wrong turn.

meaning: A pair of legs (儿) stands on ice (冫) while someone says (言) an order — you must follow the command carefully, like stepping on thin ice.
reading: チョウ — Picture a waiter taking your order and writing 'CHOU' on his pad — the sound of a precise order.

meaning: Evening (夕) falls, and someone says (言) goodbye — the words part you from the day, like a farewell that splits you from a group.
reading: シ — Imagine a person saying 'SHI!' as they part ways at evening (夕) — a sharp, short sound of separation.
